thread.title: How to Tell a Legitimate Mover From a Rogue One Before You Sign
thread.title_full: How to Tell a Legitimate Mover From a Rogue One Before You Sign

author: Danny Tran
title: How to Tell a Legitimate Mover From a Rogue One Before You Sign
text:
1 days ago As of September 2026, the moving industry still runs on the same split: some companies do the careful, boring paperwork right, and some skip it to lock you into a bad deal. Here's the short version. A legitimate mover checks your things in person or by video before handing you a written estimate, tells you plainly whether that estimate is binding or non-binding, and never asks you to sign anything with blank spaces on it. A rogue mover quotes you a number over the phone and leaves the details fuzzy on purpose.
Get more than one bid before you decide anything — the federal moving checklist says to get estimates from at least three movers or brokers so you can compare cost and services side by side.
Ask local movers for a written, signed estimate . Tell local movers about your move, and qualified pros call you to go over an estimate, free and no obligation. “I need movers who give a written binding estimate before I sign.” → Free for homeowners · Your number stays private Before you call: what to have ready Before you pick up the phone, get a few things straight in your own head.
Plan on getting estimates from at least three movers or brokers, not just one. Know whether you're hiring a moving company directly or a broker — the two aren't the same, and mixing them up can cost you. Expect any interstate mover to hand you a federal booklet called Your Rights and Responsibilities When You Move — it's required, not optional. Think about whether the standard liability coverage, 60 cents per pound, is enough for what you own, or whether you want fuller coverage. Federal law requires interstate movers to offer liability coverage options, so ask about them. Where to look and what to check Confirm the mover has a U.S. DOT number — it's required for interstate movers, and it should show up in their advertising. Search FMCSA's official mover database for registration status, insurance information, and complaint history. Check the mover and broker's record with the Better Business Bureau too. If a company's ads don't show a U.S. DOT number anywhere, treat that as a warning sign, not an oversight. The questions to ask on the call Will someone come look at my things in person or by video before you give me a written estimate? Is this estimate binding or non-binding, and what does that mean for my final bill? If the actual weight comes in higher than you estimated, what happens to the price? Can I get the estimate in writing, signed, with nothing left blank? What a good answer sounds like A careful mover explains the difference without being asked twice. A binding estimate locks in the total cost of the move based on the items and services listed on the estimate — you do not have to pay more than that amount at delivery. A non-binding estimate is just what the company believes the move will cost, based on estimated weight and the services you've asked for; it doesn't lock in your final costs the way a binding one does. If you go with non-binding, the company is legally capped at charging 110 percent of that estimate at delivery — not more, no matter what surprises come up. If a company can't say which type of estimate they're giving you, that's not a good answer.
Red flags that end the conversation They give you a price over the phone or by email, with no one ever inspecting your things in person or by video. FMCSA specifically warns that rogue movers typically offer low estimates this way. If the mover is within 50 miles of you and still won't do an on-site estimate, that's worth pushing back on. They ask you to sign an estimate or inventory sheet that's blank or mostly empty. Dishonest movers use those blanks later to fill in whatever they want. Signing blank paperwork has let dishonest movers inflate the final cost to two to three times the original quote — that's the real cost of skipping this check. Anything you're asked to sign should have no unfilled blanks except the actual weight or in-transit charges, which legitimately can't be known yet. When to stop checking and ask the mover directly Once you've confirmed registration and gotten your written, signed estimate, the remaining questions are ones only the mover can answer for your specific move: what type of liability coverage they're offering, and whether your estimate is binding or non-binding in writing, not just spoken. FMCSA's rules here cover interstate movers. If your move stays inside one state, the rules can be different — check with your state or local government for what applies where you live.
